text: Knowing when rice is ready to harvest (ការកំណត់ពេលប្រមូលផលស្រូវ) requires checking grain maturity across several parts of the field, not one panicle. Mature panicles turn predominantly yellow/straw-colored (ពណ៌លឿង/ពណ៌ចំបើង) and grains become firm rather than soft or milky; a moisture meter (ឧបករណ៍វាស់សំណើមគ្រាប់ស្រូវ) is useful where available but should not be treated as required, since many smallholders don't own one. Do not use a single fixed harvest-moisture number as a universal rule -- the right target depends on variety, harvesting method, and drying capacity available immediately after cutting. Harvesting too early leaves immature, chalky grain; harvesting too late exposes the standing crop to lodging, shattering, birds, insects, and rain. This matters especially at the wet-to-dry season transition: watch the weather forecast and organize labor, transport, threshing, and drying rather than waiting for the whole field to look visually uniform. Rice varieties differ substantially in maturity duration (roughly 120-140 days for shorter-duration varieties up to 170-200 days for some traditional/long-duration ones), so never calculate a harvest date from planting date alone without also knowing the variety and production system. If the farmer doesn't know their variety, fall back on observable maturity indicators (grain color and firmness) rather than assuming a variety. Treat harvesting and drying capacity as one combined decision: there's little benefit to harvesting quickly if there's nowhere suitable to dry the grain afterward, so ask 'is rain expected soon, and where will you dry the rice after threshing?' before advising a farmer to harvest now.
